Joe DiMaggio was an outfielder and one of baseball's most complete players, starring for the Yankees from nineteen thirty-six to nineteen fifty-one. His grace, consistency, and fifty-six-game hitting streak in nineteen forty-one made him an icon of the sport's golden age, and his quiet, dignified demeanor off the field elevated his cultural standing beyond baseball.

In nineteen forty-one, DiMaggio achieved a fifty-six-game hitting streak, the longest in major league history by twelve games, and it is considered one of baseball's most unbreakable records. He hit three twenty-five lifetime and drove in one thousand five hundred thirty-seven runs; a career on-base plus slugging of point nine seventy-seven places him among the all-time greats. DiMaggio won three American League MVP awards in nineteen thirty-nine, nineteen forty-seven, and nineteen forty-eight, and was a thirteen-time All-Star. He played thirteen seasons with the Yankees and won ten American League pennants and nine World Series championships.

Nicknamed Joltin' Joe and The Yankee Clipper, he epitomized elegance and power in the same player. DiMaggio succeeded Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig as the franchise's marquee star, anchoring the Yankees through the nineteen forties. Babe Ruth was the Yankees legend he followed and matched in stature. Lou Gehrig was his predecessor on the Yankees and a model of consistency. Mickey Mantle, the player who followed him, became the Yankees' next superstar. These legends, along with DiMaggio, defined the Yankees franchise and elevated his fame.
